newsitem.title: UK: Nickel price falls as market ponders fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: Nickel price falls as market ponders fundamentals.

text.p: Nickel prices tumbled to five-month lows on Monday against a background of ample supplies and concerns about future stainless steel output, analysts said.
Three months metal shed some $300 from Friday's kerb close to well below $7,000 per tonne after funds baled out of the market, triggering sell stops.
Speculative selling escalated on Friday after a tentative labour deal at Canadian nickel giant Inco Ltd averted a strike.
In the absence of a work disruption, recent fundamental news offers little news to cheer bulls, analysts said.
Burgeoning Russian exports have been dampening the market and will continue to do so barring a run-down of Russian stocks.
"With the Russian shipping season well under way, further gains in stocks are likely over the next few months, compounding recent losses," brokers GNI said.
Official statistics last week showed Russia's first-quarter nickel exports to non-CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) countries jumping by 48 percent year-on-year to 50,300 tonnes.
Russia's Norilsky Nikel group said on Monday nickel production was 9.2 percent higher in the first five months of 1997 than in the same year-ago period.

Western world nickel mine output is also buoyant in all the major origins, the International Nickel Study Group (INSG) said in its latest bulletin. March output was 61,300 tonnes, the highest monthly total since last June.
Paradoxically, Western world stainless steel production climbed strongly by 10.3 percent in the first quarter of the year, brokers Macquarie said in a report.
"Current indications are that the current quarter will be even higher," it said. But that trend may not be sustained later in the year," it added.
"The big worry for the market...is weaker stainless production in H2 1997," Macquarie said.

Traders in Japan last week expressed concern about a decline in demand after Sumitomo Metal Industries Ltd. decided to reduce stainless steel output by 10 percent in the April-June quarter in an attempt to boost domestic market prices.
The persistant availability of secondary nickel, despite expectations that scrap supplies would tighten, has led also some physical traders to speculate about a new source of scrap.
Macquarie noted that the large rise in the use of secondary nickel by nickel producers appeared to result from a build-up of scrap stocks from mid-1995 to mid-1996.
